https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c07r.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Students and staff at Purja's former school lit candles in commemoration of him By Koh Ewe Published 3 hours ago Tributes are pouring out across Nepal after an avalanche killed all 10 members of an expedition on Pakistan's Broad Peak, six of whom were Nepalese. Among them was Nirmal Purja, also known as Nims, a British-Nepali climber most known for climbing the world's 14 tallest peaks in just over six months. His death has sent shockwaves through the global mountaineering community and through Nepal, where he is a celebrated figure for giving a spotlight to Nepali climbing guides. Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah was among those who paid tribute, saying his "history of courage, dedication and contribution will always remain inspiring". In a moving tribute on Facebook, Purja's brother Kamal wrote: "I feel as though I have lost my whole world. My brother was not only my younger brother - he was my heart." "Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added. At the Small Heaven School in Chitwan district, near Kathmandu, which Purja had once attended, students and staff lit candles and mourned his death. Sarbagya Paudel, one of the students at the vigil, said Purja's "bravery has set a great example for our school. Not only has he made our school proud, but he has also brought pride to Nepal". Purja is still fondly remembered by those who had known him from his schooling days. Shailendra Baral, his school hostel supervisor, told AFP that as a young boy Purja had been "fearless and committed to achieving something". "He was honest and an obedient student, which made us happy. We found courage in him even when he was a child." Bahadur Panta, Purja's school friend, said he had prayed for the mountaineer through "sleepless nights" after news broke of his disappearance. "It was not only me and my friends. I think people all over the world who knew him... prayed for him. But it was his fate, no one could avoid it," he told AFP. Social media was also awash with tributes to Purja, with many saying that Nepal was in mourning and that the country had lost a "legend" and "many great climbers". "Their legacy will live on," said one comment. Purja was catapulted into international stardom after his journey was documented in a 2021 Netflix documentary. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bahadur Panta was a friend of Purja's in school Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, He was among dozens that gathered at the Small Heaven school in Chitwan Among his 10-member expedition on Broad Peak, there were six Nepali climbers. The other four climbers were from the US, China, Oman, Pakistan. They had gone missing after being caught in an avalanche last Thursday on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak. Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit. Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives. Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievements in extreme high-altitude mountaineering. Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military. But as he became more famous, troubling allegations emerged about his conduct. In 2024, a New York Times article detailed sexual allegations two women made against Purja. One alleged that he had sexually assaulted her in a hotel room in 2023 and another said he had grabbed and propositioned her while guiding her on an expedition to K2 in 2022. He denied these claims through his lawyer. Body of mountaineer Nirmal Purja recovered after Pakistan avalanche Published 23 hours ago Who is Nirmal Purja, the famed mountaineer killed in Broad Peak avalanche? Published 20 hours ago But while Purja may be the most recognisable face, he was not the only famed climber in the disaster-hit expedition on Broad Peak. The 10-member team also consisted of big names in Nepal's climbing community. There was Pur Bahadur Gurung - also known as Yukta - who summitted Everest 10 times. In 2024, he was part of the team that discovered a century-old shoe on the world's tallest peak, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on Everest with George Mallory in 1924. "Standing with you on the summit of Mount Everest is a memory I will cherish forever," fellow mountaineer and guide Uttam Lapraki wrote in a tribute to Yukta on social media. "The Himalayas have lost one of their finest sons, but your courage, kindness, and legacy will continue to inspire generations of climbers." Another member of the team, Kili Pemba Sherpa, was part of a historic 2021 expedition that summitted K2, the world's second-highest peak, in winter. That expedition was made up of all Nepali climbers, including Purja. Imagine Nepal, an expedition company where Kili Pemba worked as a guide, wrote on Instagram that he had "stood with us from the very beginning, from the days we first started climbing together". "He was humble in every way and never tired of helping climbers when they needed him. He was a foundation of our team and a part of every summit we have ever celebrated." http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27921.text: Big News Network.com Hungarian nuclear reactor temporarily shut down as Danube drops to record low BUDAPEST, July 29 (Xinhua) -- The third unit of Hungary's Paks Nuclear Power Plant has been temporarily shut down as the Danube River dropped to record low amid prolonged drought and extreme heat, an official announced on Wednesday. Istvan Kapitany, Hungary's Minister of Economy and Energy, stated on social media that the reactor shutdown was executed in accordance with predetermined operational safety guidelines as river levels continued to fall. The water level of the Danube River in Budapest fell to a record low of 31 centimeters on Tuesday, according to Hungary's General Directorate of Water Management. The shutdown followed earlier curtailments at the facility, which comprises four units with a combined capacity of around 2,000 megawatts. The minister said the shutdown was part of a carefully prepared plan prioritizing operational safety rather than an unexpected emergency. The plant relies on the Danube for cooling water, making flow reductions necessary to meet environmental regulations regarding water temperature. The temporary electricity deficit will be compensated by domestic renewable energy sources and increased power imports, Kapitany added, reassuring the public that Hungary's energy grid remains stable. https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: BERLIN — It’s not the kind of photo op German Chancellor Friedrich Merz would likely want to frame for his office wall: him standing next to Ulrich Siegmund , the far-right politician a national magazine recently labeled the country’s “ most dangerous man .” And yet, such a picture might soon be hard for Merz to avoid. On Sept. 6, Siegmund is set for a sweeping victory in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. If his far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party secures an outright majority in the state parliament, Siegmund will likely become premier, and his party will have broken through the political “firewall” that has kept it out of all federal and state governments since its founding in 2013. It would be a historic triumph for the AfD and a shock to Germany’s political system. Advertisement Advertisement As premier, one of Siegmund’s earliest duties would be to take over the annually rotating chair position of the regular conferences of Germany’s 16 state premiers. The role usually comes with a visit to Berlin and a joint appearance with the chancellor before the press. Calling this uncharted territory would be an understatement. “The AfD is questioning the fundamental decisions made by the Federal Republic of Germany since 1949,” Merz once said . The chancellor is not alone in his concern. All other major parties, and large parts of the German media, see the AfD as a threat to the country’s liberal postwar order. Yet, if the party takes power in a state for the first time, the political establishment will no longer be able to keep it at arm’s length. While normal relations may be out of the question, at least for the foreseeable future, Germany’s federal system requires a minimum of cooperation and mutual support. So how would the German establishment deal with a state governed by the AfD? POLITICO put this question to officials in the federal government and several state governments. The reluctance to answer was striking, especially among Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union. Senior party figures and state ministers either refused to comment or would not be quoted by name. The hesitation is understandable. The CDU and the CSU once owned the political space to the right of center. Today, the AfD is eating into it . State ministers from both the Social Democrats and the Greens were more prepared to discuss strategy on the record. Advertisement Advertisement The conversations for this article were dominated by a single concern: domestic security, especially the protection of intelligence information, given the AfD’s advocacy for closer ties with President Vladimir Putin’s Russia. According to Social Democrat Georg Maier , who serves as the state of Thuringia’s interior minister, Siegmund’s party has “good channels” to Moscow. “If the AfD provides the minister-president in Saxony-Anhalt, the champagne corks will be popping in the Kremlin,” he told POLITICO. AfD supporters listen to Siegmund during a campaign event in Dessau-Roßlau, Germany, on Aug. 19, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images Although there is no playbook yet for containing an AfD government, the thinking in Berlin and several state capitals has already moved well beyond the abstract. Option 1: Hold extra informal meetings One way to limit the AfD’s access to sensitive discussions could be to simply have more discussions. In addition to the gathering of state premiers that Siegmund would be expected to chair for a year, Germany’s states regularly coordinate through a network of ministerial “conferences.” Among the most important is the conference of interior ministers, where some of the country’s most pressing security and intelligence matters are discussed. One possibility being considered is to keep holding the regular meetings of the interior ministers but also organize separate gatherings for particularly sensitive issues. Only Germany’s 15 other interior ministers would attend these meetings, without the representative from Saxony-Anhalt. Several ministers confirmed this hypothetical scenario to POLITICO. The idea builds on a long-established practice in German politics. State governments are informally grouped into so-called “A” and “B” states, depending on which political camp holds the governing majority: Social Democratic-led governments on one side, conservative governments on the other. Before major conferences, both camps coordinate internally. Advertisement Advertisement Applied to the AfD, this model would put the ostracized government on one side and everyone else on the other. Christoph Degenhart , a professor emeritus of constitutional law and former judge at Saxony’s Constitutional Court, said the idea is definitely conceivable. “How long that would work and whether the courts would tolerate it is, of course, another question.” Option 2: Erect a wall One of the biggest worries regarding the AfD is its closeness to Moscow, according to Maier. Specifically, the minister’s biggest concern is an AfD-led interior ministry. Whoever runs such a department, he said, gains access to highly classified information. And yet, excluding the entire state from Germany’s domestic intelligence network would not be possible; public safety, including protection against terrorist attacks, would rule that out. “But we can build Chinese walls into our joint information systems, barriers that block certain information,” said the minister. He laughed briefly. “‘Chinese walls’ fits perfectly here. The AfD doesn’t just have a soft spot for Moscow,” he added. What information would Maier wall off? “We would have to keep all intelligence relating to right-wing extremism and the entire area of espionage away from the AfD,” he said. Such a “preventive segmentation” would be legally possible, he added, citing legal advice he has obtained. It could also be implemented relatively quickly. “Government formation is not going to happen overnight,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement Patrick Harr, a spokesperson for the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch, rejected all accusations of closeness to Russia. “That’s complete nonsense,” he said. “We don’t have a red telephone to Moscow.” “We talk to everyone, whether West or East,” he added. “That doesn’t mean we’re going to hand over files. Anyone who claims otherwise is talking nonsense. If and when we get access to such information, we understand our responsibility as a party of government.” But Konstantin von Notz , a Green member of the Bundestag and deputy chair of its intelligence oversight panel, pointed to Austria’s far-right Freedom Party’s (FPÖ) time in government as a cautionary example. After entering government in 2017, the FPÖ took control of the interior ministry. The following year, police raided Austria’s domestic intelligence service and seized sensitive data, including information from allied agencies. Thorsten Frei, right, Friedrich Merz, center, and Markus Söder, left, speak to media in Berlin on July 29, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images Western intelligence partners then restricted the sharing of confidential information , while Austria’s service temporarily pulled back from working groups of the Bern Club — an informal network of Western intelligence services, officially on a voluntary basis. Germany could face something similar under an AfD government, said von Notz, if for example the country’s allies suspected Russia would be able to access the database used by Germany’s domestic intelligence services to exchange information on extremists, spies and other security threats. “The British, the Americans, the Poles, the Ukrainians — nobody would share information with us anymore for fear that everything would be passed on to Moscow,” warned the Green politician. Advertisement Advertisement Option 3: Cut off their funds Another instrument mentioned both by AfD figures and the party’s opponents is Germany’s fiscal equalization system, which helps poorer states with money from wealthier ones and additional federal funds. Saxony-Anhalt has depended on this system for decades. In 2025, it received around €2.8 billion according to preliminary figures — nearly one-fifth of its state budget. Reducing or even halting such payments would be one way to make life harder for an AfD government, or to coerce the party to behave in ways the political establishment finds acceptable. Within the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch, this scenario is seen as a real risk. The legal hurdles, however, would be high. Danyal Bayaz , the Green finance minister of Baden-Württemberg, one of Germany’s wealthier contributor states, chose his words carefully. “The fiscal equalization system is anchored in the constitution and is not an instrument that can simply be changed according to the political weather,” he said. He then added a caveat: A federal state based on solidarity, said Bayaz, depends on shared commitments to the rule of law. If a state government were to call those principles into question, or pursue legally dubious special paths, that would affect trust and cooperation with the federal government and other states, “including in financial matters.” Bayaz’s spokesperson stressesdthat this was the minister’s personal assessment, not an agreed position of the state government — a coalition led by the Greens, with the CDU as its junior partner. Advertisement Option 4: Deploy the nuclear option The most powerful constitutional instrument would be Bundeszwang , or federal coercion. Under Article 37 of Germany’s Basic Law, the federal government, with the consent of the Bundesrat — the chamber representing the states — may take “necessary measures” to compel a state to fulfill its legal obligations. In plain English: Berlin could force a state government to obey federal law. The provision has never been used. In the reporting for this story, no one interviewed brought it up on their own — perhaps out of conviction, perhaps out of fear that merely mentioning it would play into the AfD’s hands before the elections. Within AfD’s right-wing intellectual circles, federal coercion has long been treated as a realistic scenario. In 2025, publisher Götz Kubitschek, whose estate lies in Saxony-Anhalt and who the New York Times once labeled “the prophet of Germany’s new right,” told POLITICO this is what he would expect to see happen. The entrance to the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Cologne, Germany is pictured on Sept. 22, 2025. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images A potential trigger can only be guessed at. If, for example, an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt failed to provide for even the most basic needs of asylum seekers, the federal government could intervene with binding orders to restore those services, eventually through a federal commissioner with the authority to issue instructions to the state and all its authorities. Would all this work? Whatever Germany’s political establishment does to contain the country’s first AfD government, this fall or later, the risks are obvious. Measures meant to defend liberal democracy could also feed the AfD’s central grievance and that of many of its voters: that the establishment refuses to accept the party even when it wins. Public opinion on this is more divided than it once was. A representative poll from July found that only 42 percent of Germans still considered it right for the Social Democrats and the CDU to refuse cooperation with the AfD; another survey showed that support for the exclusion strategy had fallen to 46 percent, down from 54 percent in early 2025 . Advertisement Doing nothing out of the ordinary may well be the safest option for established parties. The AfD has spent years thriving in opposition, turning its rivals’ mistakes and broken promises into political fuel. But it has never governed. Once in office, it could become mired in incompetence and internal infighting, sparing its opponents the need for special defensive maneuvers. Key figures in the AfD’s own orbit are aware of this danger. “They have to prepare like the biggest overachievers,” Kubitschek told POLITICO in 2025 regarding Siegmund’s state party. Benedikt Kaiser , another influential far-right intellectual and aide to an AfD member of the Bundestag, also advised caution if the party wins an outright majority: “In the first 90 days of government, the AfD has to pursue a politics that does not create fear,” he said, mentioning “family benefits, free school meals, things like that” as examples. Even as Germany’s political establishment considers ways to contain an AfD state government, the party’s intellectual leaders are fretting over a more immediate concern: Simply governing could prove a more effective constraint on the party than any measure the country’s political mainstream can devise.

https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/dis.text: The Budapest Times District mayor to Karácsony: don’t take back what’s working Péter Szentgyörgyvölgyi, the mayor of the 5th district, wrote an open letter to Dávid Vitézy, Minister of Transport and Investment, and to Gergely Karácsony, Lord Mayor of Budapest, after a proposal emerged that would return several important district public spaces to the management of the capital. In his open letter published on Facebook, Péter Szentgyörgyvölgyi (Fidesz-KDNP) wrote that there is no justification for the capital to manage the administrative areas in question, “especially since the capital would in no way be able to use the revenues generated from the management of public spaces better and more fairly than the 5th district municipality does, given that the district currently allocates 100 percent of those revenues to the high-quality operation and maintenance of public spaces.” Should the proposal — previously put out for public consultation by the government — be adopted, the Budapest municipality would become the manager of Vörösmarty Square, Széchenyi István Square, Podmaniczky Frigyes Square, and József Attila Street; the areas in question were handed over to the 5th district by the previous government four years ago. In his open letter, Péter Szentgyörgyvölgyi deemed it insufficient that observations on the proposal can only be submitted until 15 August. The mayor called for a prior needs assessment to be conducted among the residents of the 5th district, and further proposed that the mayor, the minister, and the Lord Mayor hold personal discussions on the proposal. The mayor recalled that Gergely Karácsony had himself previously stated that the correct principle of social organisation and decision-making is for every decision to be made at the lowest possible level at which the necessary information and capacity for implementation are still available. “For my part, I can confidently say: over the past nearly four years, the management of operational tasks by the Belváros Local Government has been more efficient and has served the public interest better than before,” said Péter Szentgyörgyvölgyi, adding that the proposal’s adoption without consulting or involving local residents could harm the interests of the district’s inhabitants. The mayor also pointed out that the squares are accessible exclusively via streets and areas owned by the 5th district. In his words, “it is not difficult to see” that uniform regulation and a consistent approach are desirable in the areas of public space use, permitting, oversight, and management. Péter Szentgyörgyvölgyi wrote that it “would also be a step that endangers the public interest” if the current unified system of management were to come to an end. https://www.whmi.com/news/fox/germany-bl.text: Germany blames Russia after explosive-laden drone found near Ukrainian cargo planes at major airport September 1, 2026 Germany closed Russia's Bonn consulate after linking Moscow to a failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Germany has accused Russia of carrying out a failed drone sabotage operation at Leipzig/Halle Airport and announced Tuesday it would close Russian diplomatic facilities, escalating tensions after investigators linked Moscow to last month's attack. Russia has denied the allegations. The Russian Embassy in Berlin called the accusation "absurd," while Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow would respond in a "mirror-image" fashion to Germany's actions. The embassy later described Berlin's measures as an "unprecedented escalation in Russian-German relations." In addition to closing Russian diplomatic facilities, Wadephul announced tighter entry restrictions for Russian nationals and additional measures targeting Russia's shadow fleet . He also said he had summoned Russia's ambassador to Germany, Sergei Nechayev. The announcement marks Germany's first public attribution of responsibility for the airport attack. Until now, Berlin had said only that "foreign powers" may have been involved, though U.S. media previously reported American officials believed Russia was responsible. Leipzig/Halle Airport is one of Europe's largest cargo hubs and serves as a logistics center for Germany's military and NATO allies. It is also home to Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft, making it a strategically important hub supporting Ukraine's cargo operations. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte backed Germany's findings, writing on X that the alliance "stands in full solidarity with Germany." "The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response," Rutte wrote. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union was preparing additional sanctions against Russia , while Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Moscow of escalating tensions across the region. The developments come as Germany has warned it faces an increasing campaign of hybrid threats targeting military , transportation and critical infrastructure. Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last week those responsible for hostile acts against Germany would "pay a price." German police separately said Tuesday they were investigating improvised explosive and incendiary devices discovered at a power substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg after a damaged power line caused a temporary outage. Authorities have not identified who planted the devices. Explore Other National and World News Stories Back to WHMI for Complete List of Current News

https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: London: Brazil's voters will choose from a field of presidential contenders with two familiar frontrunners on Sunday - President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro - in a closely watched race.The contest is one of several remaining races out of some 40 worldwide this year that could impact financial markets.Here's a look at the coming elections in focus for financial markets, and a roundup of those that have already happened:BRAZILPolls show incumbent Lula and Flavio, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, are neck-and-neck, and an October 25 runoff is likely.Read more: In Brazil, frustration over cost of living undermines Lula's reelection bidFlavio has sought to capitalise on cost-of-living concerns. Investors are broadly positive about Brazil, but fiscal worries, underpinned by rising spending, are the main issue. Fiscal fundamentals are the most concerning risk of a potential Lula re-election, and current (bond) spreads do not price that risk, said Ninety One portfolio manager Christine Reed.Still, only a small portion of Brazil's spending is discretionary, meaning lasting adjustments would have to reach pensions, payrolls or social benefits.Capital Economics said a Flavio win could boost equities between 10% and 20% and pull local currency bond yields down, while a Lula victory could lead to equity underperformance.ISRAEL Israeli voters will select members of the country's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset, in October 27 elections.Polls suggest a defeat for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but no single party has ever won an outright majority, and a coalition typically forms governments.Israel's economy has proved remarkably resilient to the Middle East conflict. But Moody's lowered its 2026 economic growth estimates, and raised its debt forecast, due to elevated geopolitical risks and fragile ceasefire agreements.The country's central bank chief warned that election winners must rein in defence-led state spending and invest more in education, infrastructure and other growth engines.USThe US November 3 midterm elections take place amid record diesel prices and surging government borrowing costs that have boosted mortgage rates.Read more: US midterm elections 2026: Trump's approval rating falls to record low as 2026 MidtermsVoters will determine whether Republicans retain control ​of both chambers of Congress or ​whether Democrats gain power to shape President Donald Trump's final ⁠two years in office.While some analysts warn a divided Congress could be bearish for the US dollar, the results of the election could impact everything from the Iran war to energy prices to Trump's erratic tariff policy efforts.NEW ZEALANDNew Zealand's reputation for political stability will be tested by bitterly fought November 7 elections, with opinion polls suggesting Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's coalition could lose power.A redefined mandate for New Zealand's central bank and policy reversals are among the prospects making investors uneasy.Key past elections:JAPANPrime Minister Sanae Takaichi's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) secured a landslide win in February elections, giving the green light for fiscal stimulus.Takaichi's ambitious spending, and Japan's worsening finances, sent benchmark government bond yields to their highest levels in decades. Takaichi has said the government hopes to cap new bond issuance at 40 trillion yen ($255 billion) for next fiscal year's budget.UKThe ruling Labour Party's heavy losses in May local elections and ​parliamentary votes in regions such as Scotland paved the way for the resignation of Prime Minister Keir Starmer.Investors are closely watching how new PM Andy Burnham and finance minister John Healey plan to boost Britain's long-term economic growth given fiscal constraints. The October 28 budget is shaping up as the next test of sentiment.Eurasia Group puts the odds of an early general election in 2027 at 35%. The uncertainty, alongside renewed political tension in France, is a headwind for the euro, which has hit its lowest levels in over a year.HUNGARYCentre-right Prime Minister Peter Magyar's victory in April elections ended the 16-year rule of right-wing leader Viktor Orban.Magyar's pledge to steer Hungary on a pro-European path - and secure the release of billions of euros in suspended European Union funding - boosted investor views of the nation's prospects and enabled significant jumps in consumer confidence.LATIN AMERICAColombia and Peru elections earlier this year added to a rightward shift in Latin America welcomed by some investors.Lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella secured a narrow victory in Colombia's June presidential election, pledging to reduce the size of the state, broaden the tax base, cut corporate taxes and restart oil exploration.In Peru, conservative Keiko Fujimori secured victory in a razor-thin June race.
